Sample text:
---
The first thing Mara repaired for the town was a bench that nobody remembered buying. It stood outside the post office, facing a brick wall. Someone had painted it green around the bolts, leaving six rusty circles like the rings left by tiny cups. When her father was alive, he used to sit there after collecting his pension, even in rain. Asked what he was looking at, he would say, “Nothing yet.” She had taken this for one of his jokes. Now, kneeling on his folded coat to undo the bolts, she found that the wall was rather good company.

There were things to see if you stayed low. At the foot of the wall grew a fern no longer than her thumb. A child's handwriting, scratched into the lowest brick, announced that ANDY CAN. Higher up, a pale rectangle showed where a notice had protected the surface from thirty years of weather. Mara was trying to decide what Andy could do when the postmaster came outside with two mugs. He set one on the pavement. “Council finally sent somebody?” he asked. “No,” she said. “Mind if I tell people they did? I've written them four letters about that bolt.”

She took the boards home in a shopping trolley. In her kitchen she laid them across two chairs and sanded until the room smelled of pencil shavings. Her father had taught her to run an old stocking along finished wood; if it caught, there was still work to do. Lacking a stocking, she sacrificed one of her sheer black socks. It snagged so often that by bedtime it resembled a small fishing net. She ate her supper standing at the sink because the chairs were occupied, and discovered she could watch the moon rise in the bowl of a spoon.

On Thursday she put the bench together again. On Friday a woman telephoned about a gate. On Saturday somebody left a toaster outside her door with an envelope containing three pounds and an apology for the crumbs. Mara returned the toaster unopened. She knew wood and hinges, and she understood the sort of plumbing that misbehaved in plain sight, but electricity seemed to her a private agreement between clever people and lightning. She kept the envelope, though, having noticed on its back a recipe for seed cake. In place of the money she left a slice wrapped in greaseproof paper.

By the end of summer she had mended a dozen gates, two cupboards, a puppet theatre and the long drawer beneath the map case in the library. The drawer was her favorite. Every time the librarian opened it, the river on the oldest map acquired another crease. Mara planed a whisper from each runner and rubbed the wood with the stub of a birthday candle. Afterward the river slid into daylight without a sound. The librarian stood there opening and closing it until a boy at the reading table looked up and asked if she needed him to fetch somebody.

People began asking Mara what she meant to do with herself, as though she had spent these months on a railway platform waiting for her life to arrive. She could not explain that she liked seeing where things wore out. A cupboard door usually sagged on the side nearest the stove, because that was where a cook reached for salt. The puppet theatre had lost a strip of velvet exactly where the dragon rested his chin between appearances. Wear gave you a picture of the person who wasn't there. Sometimes, of course, all it gave you was a loose screw.

In October the council sent a truck to collect the bench. Mara happened to be buying stamps. Through the post office window she saw two men in orange jackets studying the bolts with an attention that felt almost affectionate. She went out holding a sheet of seabirds, each worth the price of a letter. The younger man showed her his work order. The bench was on a list of street furniture to be replaced. Its replacement, already in the truck, was black, made of recycled plastic and shaped so rain would run straight off. “Sensible,” Mara admitted, surprising them both.

They let her have the old one, but there was nowhere in her kitchen for a bench, and her garden was a passage wide enough for one determined bicycle. For a week it stood in the postmaster's garage beside a broken rowing machine. Then Andy, who turned out to be a retired midwife named Andrea, suggested the ferry landing. “I used to sit on the ground there,” she said. “These days I can get down all right, but getting up creates a public spectacle.” They borrowed the library van and carried the bench down to the water on a Sunday.

It faced the estuary now. There were cormorants on the pilings and a red buoy that leaned sideways at the turn of the tide, as if listening for an answer under the water. Mara tried out each end of the seat. The view was certainly better, but she missed the fern, and she wondered who would notice when frost finally loosened that scratched brick. Andrea sat down beside her, bringing the smell of peppermints. For a while neither spoke. Across the channel someone was hanging white sheets on a line; the wind filled them one by one, like square sails.

“What was it you could do?” Mara asked at last. Andrea considered. She said there had been a boy, perhaps, or a spelling test. Possibly she had only wanted to scratch something into a wall and had been interrupted before she finished. “Andy can what?” Mara said. “Well, precisely.” The ferry came in, lowering its ramp onto the wet concrete. A cyclist rolled ashore with yellow flowers sticking out of his pannier. Andrea moved her bag so he could sit between them. He did, and for the next ten minutes all three watched the empty boat go back for somebody.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet, closely observed story builds around Mara’s repair work and the small community that gathers around it.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and attentive to wear, awkwardness, and modest acts of care. Mara learns to read the lives implied by a sagging cupboard door, a worn patch of velvet, or a scratched message on a wall; repairing things becomes a way of noticing people without claiming to fully understand them. The story’s pathos stays restrained: her father’s habit of sitting before a blank wall lingers, and the meaning of “ANDY CAN” remains unresolved. The reader is invited to slow down and see usefulness, companionship, and even uncertainty in overlooked places.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds ordinary repair, traces left by absent people, and the movement from solitary care toward shared public space. Its recurring objects—the bench, the scratched brick, the drawer, the ferry—carry attention between memory and present-day community. The moral emphasis is modest: practical care matters, but it does not need to solve every mystery or make everything pristine.

## Evidence line
> Wear gave you a picture of the person who wasn't there.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The coherent, distinctive pattern of patient observation and unsentimental communal care recurs across the repairs, objects, and unresolved ending.
